summary.text: **Biologics** target the cascade — TNF (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab), IL-6 (tocilizumab), B cells (rituximab), T-cell costimulation (abatacept) — and all DMARDs share **infection risk**: screen for TB and hepatitis, vaccinate first.

chunks.text: **Nociceptive pain:** direct activation of pain receptors by tissue injury.
**Inflammatory pain:** pain driven by inflammatory mediators.
**Neuropathic pain:** pain from nerve injury or dysfunction.
**Acute pain:** recent onset, often tied to an identifiable injury or flare.
**Chronic pain:** persists beyond expected healing time, often > 3 months. Treatment approach differs sharply between acute and chronic pain.
**Tissue injury → release of inflammatory mediators → sensitization of nociceptors → pain.**
Key mediators: **prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6).**
Arachidonic acid → COX enzyme → prostaglandins → pain and inflammation: the spine of the acetaminophen, NSAID, and corticosteroid sections.
**NSAIDs and COX-2 inhibitors act at the COX step; glucocorticoids act further upstream; cytokine inhibitors and analgesics act through separate, parallel pathways.**
**Corticosteroids block phospholipase A₂** (membrane phospholipids → arachidonic acid), so a broad range of mediators falls. NSAIDs block only COX, so they lower prostaglandins specifically.
**Nociceptor sensitization:** injury releases PGE2, bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines, which **lower the pain threshold** — normally harmless stimuli now hurt.
Prostaglandins sensitize nociceptors, so they are the main NSAID target; bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines are not blocked by NSAIDs.
Where drugs act: NSAIDs block COX; corticosteroids block PLA2 (phospholipase A₂) one step upstream.
**The immune response:** chronic inflammation involves eicosanoids, leukotrienes, cytokines, chemokines, and many immune cells; RA, SLE, vasculitis, and gout all stem from this cascade.
The lipoxygenase branch of arachidonic acid makes leukotrienes (chemotaxis, bronchoconstriction, vascular permeability) — a separate branch from the COX step NSAIDs block.
Most musculoskeletal pain in this lecture is a mix of nociceptive and inflammatory; pure neuropathic pain belongs to a separate pharmacology unit.
The mediator list is the roadmap for the lecture: NSAIDs target prostaglandins, biologic DMARDs target specific cytokines.

**Therapeutic strategies:** goal 1 is symptom relief and function (NSAIDs and DMARDs); goal 2 is slowing tissue damage, for which DMARDs are absolutely necessary. Response is tracked with indices such as DAS28 in RA.
Corticosteroids (block phospholipase A₂) vs. NSAIDs and COX-2 inhibitors (block COX): two distinct points of intervention.
Corticosteroids act **upstream** at phospholipase A₂, not at COX — that is why their effect is broader than an NSAID’s.
The lecture’s drugs target nociceptive and inflammatory pain; neuropathic pain is a different unit.
Drug class: Corticosteroids · Step it blocks: **Phospholipase A₂** (upstream) · What falls: A broad range of mediators

chunks.text: Why are corticosteroids broader than NSAIDs? They act at phospholipase A₂, before arachidonic acid is released, so every mediator made from it falls — NSAIDs only stop the COX branch.
Mediators that make pain: **P-B-H-C** — **P**rostaglandins, **B**radykinin, **H**istamine, **C**ytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6).
Effective analgesia, with a narrow margin in overdose: treats pain and fever well, but is **not an anti-inflammatory drug** the way NSAIDs are.
Acetaminophen leaves inflammation alone; NSAIDs go after it directly.
Acetaminophen (the lecture’s single non-NSAID analgesic).
**Analgesic effect:** relieves mild-to-moderate pain, with a central mechanism that is still incompletely understood.
**Antipyretic effect:** reduces fever via central effects on the hypothalamic temperature-regulating center.
**Anti-inflammatory effect:** minimal at the periphery — unlike NSAIDs, acetaminophen is not a reliable anti-inflammatory agent.
**Mechanism:** analgesia and antipyresis are mainly central, via reduced CNS prostaglandin synthesis; peripheral anti-inflammatory action is minimal.
Textbook adds: a weak peripheral COX-1/COX-2 inhibitor whose pain relief also involves opioid, cannabinoid, and serotonergic systems.
Reasonable first-line for mild osteoarthritis pain.
Generally safer first-line than an NSAID in a patient with NSAID red flags (kidney disease, anticoagulation, older age).
Preferred over aspirin in aspirin allergy, hemophilia, peptic ulcer history, or aspirin-induced bronchospasm; alone it is inadequate for inflammatory conditions such as RA.
**Overdose: glutathione stores are depleted, NAPQI accumulates, and hepatocyte injury follows.**
**Overdose cascade:** glucuronidation/sulfation saturate → more drug shunted to CYP2E1 → more NAPQI, glutathione exhausted → NAPQI binds hepatocyte proteins → **centrilobular liver necrosis**.
Ingesting 15 g may be fatal (centrilobular hepatic necrosis); take care with liver disease, heavy alcohol use, or malnutrition.
**Pearl:** chronic alcohol use and fasting lower GSH and raise risk; both also induce CYP2E1.
**Hidden overdose:** many combination cold, flu, and sleep products also contain acetaminophen — **unintentional double-dosing is a leading cause of acetaminophen-related liver injury.**
Combining acetaminophen with an NSAID improves pain control but can potentiate the NSAID’s GI toxicity.
Normal handling: acetaminophen → NAPQI (toxic metabolite) → glutathione conjugation → safe excretion.
NAPQI = N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine — the “toxic metabolite” example from Lecture 1’s drug-metabolism section.
**Major route (~90%):** glucuronidation and sulfation → safe urinary excretion.
**Minor route (~5–10%):** CYP2E1 oxidation → NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone-imine), normally neutralized by glutathione (GSH) conjugation at therapeutic doses.
Mostly conjugated to inactive sulfate and glucuronide; half-life 2–3 hours, relatively unaffected by renal function.
**Always ask about ALL sources of acetaminophen.**
Patients often don’t realize a product contains acetaminophen unless they check the label — reinforce generic-name awareness.
**Acute single ingestion:** plot the acetaminophen level on the **Rumack-Matthew nomogram**; check AST/ALT.
**How to use the nomogram:** draw a level at 4 hours or later after a single acute ingestion and plot it against time since ingestion.
**Above the treatment line:** give NAC. **Below the line:** toxicity unlikely. Example: 8 h, 120 mcg/mL is above the line, so start NAC.
The illustrative treatment line runs from 150 mcg/mL at 4 h, halving every 4 h, to 4.7 mcg/mL at 24 h.
**Limits:** not valid before 4 hours, with an unknown ingestion time, or for staggered, repeated supratherapeutic, or chronic ingestion — use clinical judgment, AST/ALT, and poison control.
Start NAC without waiting if presentation is late or the level is unavailable and the ingestion is significant.
After 24 hours the nomogram is not used: 4.7 mcg/mL is only where the treatment line ends, not a safe cutoff. A detectable level or elevated AST/ALT guides NAC, per protocol or poison control.
Adults: generally no more than 4 g/day — and even 4 g is associated with more liver function test abnormalities.
**Antidote: N-acetylcysteine**, a glutathione precursor — it replenishes glutathione to detoxify NAPQI.
Case: a patient on regular acetaminophen for back pain starts an OTC cold-and-flu combination. **What is the hidden danger in this combination?** Double-dosing acetaminophen.
**Antidote: NAC (N-acetylcysteine) replenishes glutathione; give early for best effect.**
Ask: “What is the danger of a cold-and-flu product on top of regular acetaminophen?” Look for unintentional double dosing from combination products.
**Other analgesics — tramadol:** weak μ-opioid agonist plus serotonin/norepinephrine reuptake inhibition; no anti-inflammatory effect; up to 300 mg/day; risks serotonin syndrome and seizures.
Pain · Acetaminophen: Yes (mild–moderate) · NSAIDs: Yes
Fever · Acetaminophen: Yes (hypothalamus) · NSAIDs: Yes
Inflammation · Acetaminophen: **Minimal — not reliable** · NSAIDs: **Yes — powerful**
Main danger · Acetaminophen: Liver (NAPQI) in overdose or double-dosing · NSAIDs: GI, renal, cardiovascular
Antidote · Acetaminophen: N-acetylcysteine · NSAIDs: Not covered in materials

chunks.text: Why does N-acetylcysteine work? Glutathione is what safely conjugates NAPQI. Overdose uses it up; N-acetylcysteine is a glutathione precursor, so it refills the supply.
Acetaminophen does **P**ain and **P**yrexia, not **P**uffiness (inflammation).
Powerful anti-inflammatory effect, with real systemic risk.
**Nonselective NSAIDs inhibit both COX-1 and COX-2.**
**Celecoxib selectively inhibits COX-2 over COX-1.**
Ibuprofen — common first-line choice for mild-moderate pain.
Naproxen — longer half-life, twice-daily dosing.
Diclofenac — available in oral and topical formulations.
Indomethacin — more potent, more GI/CNS adverse effects.
**Ketorolac — short-term use only, significant GI/renal risk.**
Celecoxib — the COX-2 selective agent.
NSAID → COX inhibition → ↓ prostaglandins → ↓ pain, inflammation, fever.
**COX-1, the “housekeeping” enzyme:** maintains gastric mucosal protection and normal renal blood flow; inhibiting it causes GI and renal adverse effects.
**COX-2:** induced mainly at sites of inflammation and the primary source of inflammatory prostaglandins; selective inhibition targets inflammation with less GI toxicity.
Simplified teaching model, not an absolute separation: COX-1 and COX-2 functions overlap, and COX-2 is also constitutively expressed in the kidney and elsewhere.
**Pathway:** COX converts arachidonic acid to prostaglandins **and thromboxane A2 (TXA2)**. Less prostaglandin: pain, fever, and inflammation fall. Less TXA2: bleeding risk.
Every NSAID shares the COX mechanism; the side effects follow from losing protective prostaglandins (GI injury, platelet inhibition, renal effects).
**COX-1 is constitutive:** gastric mucosa (protection), platelets (TXA2, clotting), kidney (renal blood flow). **COX-2 is inducible** in inflamed tissue: pain, swelling, fever.
Nonselective NSAIDs block both isoforms, so GI injury is common. Selectivity trades anti-inflammatory benefit against GI and platelet protection.
Celecoxib selectively inhibits inducible COX-2, the main source of inflammatory prostaglandins, and largely spares COX-1 in gastric mucosa — lowering ulcer and bleeding risk.
**Celecoxib’s trade-off:** PGI2 (prostacyclin) falls without a matching drop in TXA2, which raises cardiovascular event risk; stomach and platelet protection continue.
Celecoxib still affects kidney prostaglandins, so renal risk is not eliminated.
Aspirin irreversibly blocks platelet COX (the effect lasts the 8–10-day life of the platelet); other nonselective NSAIDs are reversible inhibitors.
COX-2 inhibitors spare platelet thromboxane (made by COX-1) but block endothelial prostacyclin — so they are not cardioprotective.
Oral NSAIDs for osteoarthritis — effective, but carry the systemic risks below.
Topical NSAIDs — effective local relief with much lower systemic exposure.
NSAIDs ease symptoms but, unlike DMARDs, do not alter the course of any arthritic disorder.
Used in RA, spondyloarthropathies, OA, sprains and strains, low back pain, and gout (tolmetin appears ineffective in gout).
**Gastrointestinal:** gastritis, peptic ulcer, GI bleeding.
**Renal:** decreased renal perfusion, fluid retention, acute kidney injury.
**Cardiovascular:** hypertension, increased risk of cardiovascular events.
**Celecoxib:** lower risk of ulcer/bleeding, but **COX-2 selectivity is associated with increased cardiovascular event risk — a key trade-off.**
Celecoxib’s renal risk is similar to nonselective NSAIDs — COX-2 selectivity does not protect the kidney.
**GI:** less prostaglandin-driven mucus and bicarbonate leaves the mucosa open to injury (ulcer, bleeding).
**Kidney:** reduced afferent arteriolar dilation lowers renal blood flow (AKI, fluid retention).
**Platelets:** reduced TXA2 impairs aggregation, increasing bleeding risk.
Beyond GI, renal, and CV: headache, tinnitus, dizziness, rare aseptic meningitis, liver test abnormalities, asthma, rashes, hyperkalemia.
Use caution or avoid in: active GI bleeding or ulcer history; chronic kidney disease; heart failure or cardiovascular disease.
Also caution or avoid with anticoagulant therapy and in late pregnancy.
Ibuprofen is relatively contraindicated with nasal polyps, angioedema, or bronchospastic reactivity to aspirin.
NSAIDs + anticoagulants → ↑ bleeding risk.
NSAIDs + ACE inhibitors/ARBs → ↑ AKI risk; add a diuretic and it is the **“triple whammy,”** a very high-yield AKI pattern.
NSAIDs + diuretics → reduced diuretic effect, ↑ renal risk.
NSAIDs + corticosteroids → ↑ GI ulcer risk.
Ibuprofen taken with aspirin blocks aspirin’s irreversible platelet inhibition, limiting its cardioprotective effect.
Celecoxib (a CYP2C9 substrate) occasionally interacts with warfarin and raises lithium and fluconazole levels.
Naproxen’s longer half-life allows twice-daily dosing; diclofenac comes as oral and topical forms.
**Chemistry & pharmacokinetics:** most NSAIDs are weak acids, well absorbed, ~98% albumin-bound, metabolized by CYP3A or CYP2C, and renally excreted.
These three systems (GI, renal, CV) are the organizing framework for every NSAID contraindication and interaction discussion (Table 1).
Highest GI-bleeding risk: celecoxib, or a nonselective NSAID plus omeprazole or misoprostol.
Case: a 72-year-old with OA, CKD, hypertension, and an anticoagulant. **Is an NSAID a good first-line choice for this patient’s pain? Why or why not?**
**Three NSAID red flags at once** — renal disease, anticoagulation, and age-related bleeding risk — make acetaminophen or a non-NSAID strategy generally safer first-line.
Celecoxib is a classic “trade one risk for another” point: a better GI profile, but not a free lunch cardiovascularly or renally.
There is no risk-free NSAID choice, only a different risk profile.
**Choice of NSAID:** all are about equally effective, so choose by toxicity, cost, and patient factors; in renal insufficiency nonacetylated salicylates may be best.

Protects / makes · COX-1: Gastric mucosa; platelet TXA₂ (clotting); renal blood flow · COX-2: Primary source of **inflammatory prostaglandins**
Blocking it causes · COX-1: GI and renal adverse effects; less clotting · COX-2: Less pain, swelling, fever (selective blockade = less GI toxicity)

chunks.text: Why do NSAIDs hurt the stomach and kidney? Blocking COX-1, the housekeeping enzyme, removes the prostaglandins that protect gastric mucosa and keep renal blood flow normal.
Why the “triple whammy”? An ACE inhibitor/ARB, a diuretic, and an NSAID each push kidney perfusion the wrong way at once — together they cause acute kidney injury.
NSAID harms = **GRC**: **G**ut, **R**enal, **C**ardiovascular (Table 1).
**Osteoarthritis (OA):** primarily degenerative joint disease — cartilage breakdown with mechanical wear.
**Rheumatoid arthritis (RA):** autoimmune, systemic inflammatory disease — immune-mediated joint destruction.
**OA pathophysiology:** mechanical load and wear degrade cartilage; bone remodels with osteophytes.
**RA pathophysiology:** immune activation → autoimmune synovitis forms a **pannus** that erodes cartilage and bone; **TNF-α and IL-6** drive the inflammation and joint damage.
OA treatment goal: pain control and function.
RA treatment goal: suppress disease activity, not just pain.
The hinge: OA is managed mainly with analgesics/NSAIDs, while RA requires disease-modifying therapy.
**DMARD (Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drug):** a drug intended to alter the course of RA, not just mask its symptoms.
**Goal of therapy:** slow or halt joint destruction and systemic inflammation, rather than providing analgesia alone.
An NSAID can make a patient feel better without changing the disease trajectory; a DMARD is meant to change the trajectory itself.
**NSAIDs** relieve pain and swelling within days but do not alter joint damage; **DMARDs** take weeks to months to act, then slow cartilage and bone destruction.
**Timing:** judge a DMARD over months, not after the first visit — set expectations that benefit builds over months. Relief now with NSAIDs, protection later with DMARDs.
Targeted therapy: each biologic class corresponds to a different cytokine or cell type in the inflammatory cascade — the mediator list from the start of the lecture.
DMARD effects take 2 weeks to 6 months to appear. Types: conventional synthetic (cs), biologic (b), and targeted synthetic (ts, e.g., tofacitinib).
Biologics are large molecules, usually proteins made by recombinant DNA technology; JAK inhibitors are oral small-molecule targeted synthetic DMARDs.
**Methotrexate — the anchor drug for most RA regimens.**
Hydroxychloroquine — milder disease; relatively favorable safety profile.
Sulfasalazine — often used in combination regimens.
Leflunomide — alternative when methotrexate is not tolerated.
Adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab — **TNF inhibitors**.
Tocilizumab — **IL-6 inhibitor**.
Rituximab — **B-cell targeted therapy**.
Abatacept — **T-cell costimulation modulator**.
**Mechanism: inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, reducing immune cell proliferation at low RA doses.** (methotrexate)
**Hydroxychloroquine** alters lysosomal and TLR signaling (less antigen signaling); **sulfasalazine** reduces cytokine and prostaglandin production.
**Leflunomide** inhibits DHODH, blocking pyrimidine synthesis (slower T-cell growth).
Conventional DMARDs act inside cells or on broad immune pathways, with a slower onset than biologics.
**Methotrexate’s folate pathway:** blocking DHFR stops dihydrofolate (DHF) → tetrahydrofolate (THF), the folate needed for purine and thymidylate (DNA) synthesis.
At low RA doses methotrexate is likely anti-inflammatory via **adenosine release**, not cytotoxicity.
TNF inhibitors block tumor necrosis factor-alpha signaling.
IL-6 inhibitors block interleukin-6 receptor signaling.
B-cell targeted therapy depletes or modulates B lymphocytes.
T-cell costimulation modulators block the second signal needed for T-cell activation.
Figure 3: abatacept acts at T-cell activation, TNF inhibitors and tocilizumab at cytokine release, rituximab at B cells — all upstream of synovial inflammation and joint destruction.
**TNF inhibitors:** antibodies (infliximab, adalimumab) and etanercept, a receptor fusion protein, neutralize soluble and membrane TNF-α, preventing TNFR activation.
**Tocilizumab** blocks both membrane and soluble IL-6 receptors.
**Abatacept (CTLA-4-Ig)** binds CD80/86 and blocks CD28 costimulation, acting early at T-cell activation.
**Rituximab (anti-CD20)** binds CD20 and depletes B cells for months.
Each biologic intercepts a different step of the immune cascade: walk it from T-cell activation to cytokines to synovial damage — abatacept acts earliest.
**OA step 1:** acetaminophen — reasonable first-line for mild OA pain.
**OA step 2:** oral NSAIDs (effective, systemic risks) or topical NSAIDs (local relief, much lower systemic exposure).
**Intra-articular corticosteroid injections:** short-term relief for flares in a single joint.
Other approaches: activity modification, physical therapy, weight management.
**Where each OA analgesic acts:** acetaminophen centrally (brain and spinal cord COX) — little anti-inflammatory effect in the joint.
Oral or topical NSAIDs block COX in joint tissue (synovium and cartilage), lowering prostaglandins, pain, and swelling.
An intra-articular steroid calms local inflammation inside the joint for fast, short-term flare relief. Choice depends on which tissue drives the pain.
Methotrexate anchors most RA regimens; leflunomide is the alternative when it is not tolerated.
Rheumatoid arthritis: they modify the disease course rather than only masking symptoms.
TNF inhibitors are the first-line biologic; tocilizumab works as monotherapy; rituximab is used after TNF-inhibitor failure.
**Glucocorticoid drugs in rheumatic diseases:** used chronically in 30–70% of RA patients; relief is prompt and dramatic, and they slow new bone erosions.
Long-term prednisone in RA: no more than 7.5 mg daily, tapered when possible — even 2.8 mg daily for over 5 years is linked to severe infections.
Intra-articular corticosteroids often relieve painful symptoms for up to several months.
Long-term glucocorticoid harms: osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, Cushing syndrome, infections, cataract, glaucoma, gastric ulcer, depression.
Methotrexate starts at 7.5 mg weekly and rises to 15–25 mg weekly; it slows new erosions in RA.
**Combination therapy with DMARDs** is now the rule when monotherapy falls short; triple therapy (methotrexate, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine) rivals etanercept plus methotrexate.
**Boxed warning — all TNF inhibitors:** possible malignancy, especially lymphoma.
**Boxed warning — all JAK inhibitors:** venous thromboembolism (DVT, PE), major adverse cardiovascular events, and cancer.
Methotrexate key adverse effects: **hepatotoxicity, bone marrow suppression, pulmonary toxicity.**
**The major safety theme across all DMARDs: immunosuppression → increased infection risk.** This holds for conventional and biologic DMARDs alike.
**Risk:** suppressed immunity lets latent TB and opportunistic infections (TB, viral, fungal) emerge.
TNF inhibitors: watch for reactivation of latent TB. Tocilizumab can raise lipids and liver enzymes. Abatacept has a generally lower infection signal.
Methotrexate’s most common toxicities are nausea and stomatitis; dose-related liver enzyme elevations are frequent.
TNF inhibitors: TB reactivation, fungal infections, hepatitis B reactivation, new or worse heart failure, demyelinating disease, lupus-like syndrome.
**Methotrexate is contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic).**
Don’t stack biologics: abatacept with a TNF inhibitor probably raises serious infections; upadacitinib with biologic DMARDs is not recommended.
Hydroxychloroquine can reduce methotrexate clearance.
Tocilizumab stimulates CYP450 — doses of cyclosporine or warfarin may need adjusting.
Methotrexate given with TNF inhibitors reduces anti-drug antibodies (infliximab, golimumab, certolizumab).
**Methotrexate is dosed weekly (not daily) — a critical patient-safety point, since daily dosing can be fatal.**
**Weekly dosing only:** daily dosing has caused fatal toxicity.
**Folate supplementation** is routinely co-prescribed with methotrexate to reduce toxicity.
Folic acid co-therapy reduces methotrexate’s liver, marrow, lung, and GI toxicity.
**Baseline screening:** e.g., tuberculosis and hepatitis B/C screening before starting biologics.
**Vaccination:** update vaccines, especially live vaccines, before starting therapy.
**Ongoing monitoring:** regular labs to catch cytopenias, hepatotoxicity, or infection early.
**Infection precautions:** counsel patients to report fevers or infection symptoms promptly.
**Screen first:** TB test (IGRA or TST) and hepatitis B and C serology before starting; check hepatitis B before rituximab.
**Vaccines:** update non-live vaccines before treatment.
**Monitor:** CBC and liver and kidney labs every 1–3 months; act early on fever or infection signs.
Folic acid or leucovorin reduces stomatitis, GI, and liver test problems but may cut methotrexate efficacy by 10–18%.
Hydroxychloroquine: baseline eye exam, then annual screening after 5 years (retinopathy).
Avoid live vaccines for up to 3 months after stopping abatacept; stop upadacitinib before a live attenuated vaccine.
A 72-year-old with OA, CKD, hypertension, and an anticoagulant: acetaminophen or a non-NSAID strategy first.
OA and RA both affect the joint but are two very different diseases — don’t give RA patients analgesia alone.
Methotrexate’s weekly dosing is one of the highest-yield patient-safety points in all of rheumatology pharmacology.
Match each generic name to its class: adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab (TNF); tocilizumab (IL-6); rituximab (B cell); abatacept (T-cell costimulation).

**Read the stem first:** it reveals the mechanism class before the drug is recalled (-mab antibody: -zumab humanized, -ximab chimeric, -umab fully human; -cept receptor fusion; -nib/-tinib kinase inhibitor; -coxib COX-2 selective; -profen, -fenac, -oxicam NSAID subclasses).
Topical diclofenac 1% gel is sold over the counter for OA and muscular pain.

1.title: Musculoskeletal Pharmacology
1.notes: Opening. Say: "Today's question is simple: how do we treat musculoskeletal pain safely? We'll follow one pathway, arachidonic acid, and see where each drug class steps in."

2.title: Learning Objectives — Session 1
2.notes:
Orient students to the arc of this session: musculoskeletal pain pathways, acetaminophen, NSAIDs, and osteoarthritis/rheumatoid arthritis pharmacotherapy including DMARDs. Tell them this is the first of two sessions on Musculoskeletal Pharmacology — Session 2 picks up with gout, skeletal muscle relaxants, and bone pharmacology on Oct 29.

Objectives. Read them aloud, then say: "By the end you should be able to choose between acetaminophen, an NSAID, and a DMARD, and defend the choice."

3.title: Required & Recommended Readings — Unit 2
3.notes:
Point students to the required and recommended texts for Unit 2 before diving into content. Katzung’s Chapters 27, 36, and 42 are the required reading for this unit; Pharmacotherapy Principles and Practice is recommended as additional support, not a substitute.

Readings: Katzung 16th ed.; the Unit 2 chapters. One sentence only.

5.title: What Causes Musculoskeletal Pain?
5.notes:
Most musculoskeletal pain in this lecture is a mix of nociceptive and inflammatory — pure neuropathic pain is more the territory of a separate pharmacology unit.

Say: "Pain is classified by mechanism (nociceptive, inflammatory, neuropathic) and by time (acute vs. chronic)."

6.title: Inflammation Drives Pain
6.notes:
This mediator list is the roadmap for the whole lecture — NSAIDs target prostaglandins, biologic DMARDs target specific cytokines.

Say: "Injury releases prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine and cytokines. These lower the nociceptor threshold, so normally harmless stimuli hurt."

7.title: Inflammatory Mediators Sensitize Nociceptors
7.notes:
Say: "Injury releases prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine and cytokines. These lower the nociceptor threshold, so normally harmless stimuli hurt."

Know: Prostaglandins sensitize nociceptors, so they are the main NSAID target.

Know: Bradykinin, histamine and cytokines are not blocked by NSAIDs.

8.title: Therapeutic Targets in the Pain Pathway
8.notes:
This single arrow chain is the conceptual spine for the acetaminophen, NSAID, and corticosteroid sections that follow. The next slide builds this out further with the specific drug classes that intervene at each step.

Say: "Corticosteroids block phospholipase A2 upstream. NSAIDs block COX one step later."

9.title: The Arachidonic Acid Pathway: Where Analgesics Act
9.notes:
This figure adds the drug layer on top of the previous flow slide: name the specific drug classes (corticosteroids vs. NSAIDs/COX-2 inhibitors) and exactly where each one interrupts the cascade.

Figure 1: Corticosteroids block phospholipase A2 upstream. NSAIDs block COX one step later.

10.title: Quick Check
10.notes: Quick check: give 30 seconds, take a show of hands, then reveal.

11.title: Answer
11.notes: Answer: corticosteroids act upstream of NSAIDs.

12.title: Quick Check
12.notes: Quick check: give 30 seconds, take a show of hands, then reveal.

13.title: Answer
13.notes:
Answer: prostaglandins are the NSAID target.

Say: "That's the pathway. Now the simplest drug on it: acetaminophen."

15.title: Acetaminophen
15.notes:
This is the single most important distinction students need: acetaminophen treats pain and fever well, but it is not an anti-inflammatory drug the way NSAIDs are.

Say: "Acetaminophen is mainly central, with analgesic and antipyretic effects and minimal peripheral anti-inflammatory action."

Know: It is not an anti-inflammatory drug.

16.title: Acetaminophen: Safe vs. Toxic Metabolism
16.notes:
Explain the major safe route first, then the minor CYP2E1 route, where NAPQI is normally neutralized by glutathione conjugation at therapeutic doses.

Say: "About 90% goes down the safe route of glucuronidation and sulfation. A small fraction goes through CYP2E1 to NAPQI, which glutathione neutralizes at normal doses."

17.title: Acetaminophen Overdose and NAC Rescue
17.notes:
Overdose saturates glucuronidation and sulfation, shunting more drug to CYP2E1 and producing more NAPQI. Once glutathione is depleted, NAPQI injures hepatocytes. Give N-acetylcysteine early.

Say: "In overdose the safe route saturates, more drug goes to CYP2E1, glutathione runs out, and NAPQI injures hepatocytes."

Know: The antidote is N-acetylcysteine (NAC), given early.

Know: Chronic alcohol use and fasting raise the risk.

Know: Use the Rumack-Matthew nomogram for acute single ingestions, and check AST/ALT.

18.title: Rumack-Matthew Nomogram: Assessing Toxicity
18.notes:
The nomogram predicts hepatotoxicity risk after a single acute ingestion; if time of ingestion is unknown or ingestion is chronic, do not rely on it. Start NAC without waiting if presentation is late or the level is unavailable and ingestion is significant.

After 24 hours the nomogram is not used: 4.7 mcg/mL is only where the treatment line ends, not a safe cutoff. Get AST/ALT; a detectable level or elevated AST/ALT guides NAC, per protocol or poison control.

19.title: Acetaminophen Toxicity
19.notes:
NAPQI = N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine. Tie this directly back to the "toxic metabolite" bullet from Lecture 1’s drug metabolism section.

Ask: "What is the danger of a cold-and-flu product on top of regular acetaminophen?" Look for: unintentional double dosing from combination products.

20.title: The Hidden Acetaminophen Overdose
20.notes:
Good moment to reinforce generic-name awareness from Lecture 1 — patients often do not realize a product contains acetaminophen unless they check the label.

Hidden overdose case (slides 18-19): see the Ask on the previous slide.

21.title: Quick Check
21.notes: Quick check: give 30 seconds, take a show of hands, then reveal.

22.title: Answer
22.notes:
Answer: NAPQI accumulation after glutathione depletion.

Say: "Acetaminophen leaves inflammation alone. NSAIDs go after it directly."

24.title: How NSAIDs Work
24.notes: Say: "NSAIDs inhibit COX, so less arachidonic acid becomes prostaglandins and thromboxane. That gives less pain, inflammation and fever."

25.title: NSAIDs Block COX and Prostaglandin Synthesis
25.notes:
Explain the COX step first; every NSAID shares this mechanism, and the side effects follow from losing protective prostaglandins.

Say: "NSAIDs inhibit COX, so less arachidonic acid becomes prostaglandins and thromboxane. That gives less pain, inflammation and fever."

26.title: COX-1 vs. COX-2
26.notes:
Stress this is a simplified teaching model, not an absolute separation — COX-1 and COX-2 functions overlap, and COX-2 is also constitutively expressed in the kidney and elsewhere.

Say: "COX-1 is the housekeeper: stomach lining, platelets, kidney. COX-2 is induced at sites of inflammation."

27.title: COX-1 vs. COX-2: Constitutive vs. Inducible
27.notes:
COX-1 keeps protective prostaglandins; COX-2 is induced by inflammation. Selectivity trades anti-inflammatory benefit against GI and platelet protection.

Say: "COX-1 is the housekeeper: stomach lining, platelets, kidney. COX-2 is induced at sites of inflammation."

Know: Nonselective NSAIDs block both, which is why GI injury is common.

28.title: Nonselective NSAIDs
28.notes: Nonselective NSAIDs: ibuprofen (first-line), naproxen (longer half-life), diclofenac, indomethacin (more GI/CNS effects), ketorolac (short-term only, significant GI/renal risk).

29.title: COX-2 Selective Inhibition: Celecoxib
29.notes:
This is a classic "trade one risk for another" teaching point — better GI profile, but not a free lunch cardiovascularly or renally.

Say: "Celecoxib spares COX-1, so the GI risk is lower. The trade-off is lower PGI2 without a matching drop in TXA2, which raises cardiovascular risk. The kidney is still affected."

30.title: Celecoxib: Sparing COX-1 While Blocking COX-2
30.notes:
Use the diagram to show that selectivity separates the GI benefit from the cardiovascular trade-off. Link back to the nonselective NSAID comparison on the previous slide.

Say: "Celecoxib spares COX-1, so the GI risk is lower. The trade-off is lower PGI2 without a matching drop in TXA2, which raises cardiovascular risk. The kidney is still affected."

31.title: Nonselective NSAIDs vs. COX-2 Selective Inhibition
31.notes:
This is the graphical version of the trade-off just described in the celecoxib bullet slide — use it to reinforce that there is no risk-free NSAID choice, only a different risk profile.

Figure 2 and trade-off summary: lower GI risk, some increase in cardiovascular risk. These risk values are illustrative, not clinical data.

32.title: Quick Check
32.notes: Quick check: give 30 seconds, take a show of hands, then reveal.

33.title: Answer
33.notes: Answer: lower GI risk, with some increase in cardiovascular risk. These risk values are illustrative, not clinical data.

34.title: NSAID Adverse Effects
34.notes:
These three systems (GI, renal, CV) are the organizing framework for every NSAID contraindication and interaction discussion that follows. Table 1.

Say: "Lose prostaglandins and you lose mucosal protection, renal afferent dilation and normal platelet function."

35.title: NSAIDs: Prostaglandin Loss and Organ Effects
35.notes:
Say: "Lose prostaglandins and you lose mucosal protection, renal afferent dilation and normal platelet function."

Know: GI (ulcer, bleeding), renal (AKI, fluid retention), cardiovascular (hypertension, events).

36.title: NSAID Contraindications & Interactions
36.notes:
The "triple whammy" (NSAID + ACEi/ARB + diuretic) is a very high-yield acute kidney injury pattern to flag explicitly.

Avoid or use caution with active GI bleeding or ulcer history, CKD, heart failure, anticoagulants, and late pregnancy.

Know (interactions): NSAID plus anticoagulant means more bleeding. NSAID plus ACE inhibitor/ARB plus diuretic is the "triple whammy" for AKI. NSAID plus corticosteroid means more GI ulcer risk.

37.title: Is an NSAID the Right First Choice?
37.notes:
Excellent exam-style vignette — ask students to name all three risk factors independently before revealing the answer.

Ask: "72 years old, CKD, hypertension, on an anticoagulant. Is an NSAID a good first choice?"

38.title: Quick Check
38.notes: Quick check: give 30 seconds, take a show of hands, then reveal.

39.title: Answer
39.notes:
Answer: no. Oral NSAIDs carry the highest combined risk. Acetaminophen or a non-NSAID approach is generally safer.

Say: "Now the same drugs in the setting of arthritis."

41.title: Osteoarthritis vs. Rheumatoid Arthritis
41.notes:
This distinction is the hinge the whole rest of the section turns on: OA is managed primarily with analgesics/NSAIDs, while RA requires disease-modifying therapy.

Say: "OA is degenerative and mechanical, with cartilage wear and bone remodeling. RA is autoimmune, with synovitis, pannus, and TNF-alpha and IL-6 driving erosion."

42.title: Osteoarthritis vs. Rheumatoid Arthritis: Pathophysiology
42.notes: Say: "OA is degenerative and mechanical, with cartilage wear and bone remodeling. RA is autoimmune, with synovitis, pannus, and TNF-alpha and IL-6 driving erosion."

43.title: Pharmacologic Treatment of Osteoarthritis
43.notes: Acetaminophen is reasonable first-line for mild pain. Topical NSAIDs give effective relief with lower systemic exposure. Intra-articular corticosteroids give short-term relief for flares. Add activity modification, physical therapy and weight management.

44.title: Where Each Analgesic Acts in Osteoarthritis
44.notes:
Match each option to its site: acetaminophen centrally, NSAIDs in synovium and cartilage, corticosteroids inside the joint. Choice depends on which tissue drives the pain.

Acetaminophen is reasonable first-line for mild pain. Topical NSAIDs give effective relief with lower systemic exposure. Intra-articular corticosteroids give short-term relief for flares. Add activity modification, physical therapy and weight management.

45.title: What Makes a Drug "Disease-Modifying"?
45.notes:
Contrast explicitly with NSAIDs: an NSAID can make a patient feel better without changing the underlying disease trajectory — a DMARD is meant to change the trajectory itself.

Say: "A DMARD changes the course of RA. An NSAID only masks symptoms."

46.title: Symptom Relief vs Slowing Joint Destruction
46.notes:
Contrast the fast, symptomatic effect of NSAIDs with the slow, structure-modifying effect of DMARDs. Set expectations that DMARD benefit builds over months.

Say: "A DMARD changes the course of RA. An NSAID only masks symptoms."

Know: DMARDs take weeks to months to work. Judge them over months, not at the first visit. The curve is a schematic, not data.

47.title: Conventional (Non-Biologic) DMARDs
47.notes: Methotrexate (anchor drug, blocks DHFR), hydroxychloroquine (milder disease), sulfasalazine, leflunomide (blocks DHODH, pyrimidine synthesis).

48.title: Conventional DMARDs: Where Each Drug Acts
48.notes:
These drugs act inside cells or on broad immune pathways, with a slower onset than biologics.

Methotrexate (anchor drug, blocks DHFR), hydroxychloroquine (milder disease), sulfasalazine, leflunomide (blocks DHODH, pyrimidine synthesis).

49.title: Methotrexate
49.notes:
Methotrexate’s weekly dosing is one of the highest-yield patient-safety teaching points in all of rheumatology pharmacology — emphasize it strongly.

Know: methotrexate is dosed WEEKLY, not daily. Daily dosing has caused fatal toxicity.

50.title: Methotrexate: Folate Pathway and Low-Dose Action
50.notes:
Walk through the diagram left to right: folate is reduced to THF through DHF, and methotrexate blocks the DHFR step. Emphasize the weekly-dosing safety point.

Give folic acid to reduce liver, marrow, lung and GI toxicity. Contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic).

51.title: Biologic DMARDs
51.notes:
Each biologic class corresponds to a different cytokine or cell type in the inflammatory cascade shown earlier in the lecture — tie this back to the mediator list from Section 1. The next slide shows these same four drug classes as a mechanism diagram.

Say: "Four classes by target." TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept), IL-6 blockers (tocilizumab), abatacept (CTLA-4-Ig, blocks CD28 costimulation), rituximab (anti-CD20, depletes B cells).

52.title: Biologic DMARDs: Mechanism by Target
52.notes:
Each biologic intercepts a different step of the immune cascade; match the target to the drug class.

Say: "Four classes by target." TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept), IL-6 blockers (tocilizumab), abatacept (CTLA-4-Ig, blocks CD28 costimulation), rituximab (anti-CD20, depletes B cells).

53.title: Biologic DMARDs: Where Each Class Intercepts the Immune Cascade
53.notes:
This is the visual counterpart to the fourCard slide just shown — have students match each generic drug name to its box on this diagram before you reveal the answer.

Figure 3: walk the cascade from T-cell activation to cytokines to synovial damage. Abatacept acts earliest.

54.title: Quick Check
54.notes: Quick check: give 30 seconds, take a show of hands, then reveal.

56.title: DMARD Safety: Immunosuppression
56.notes: Say: "The theme is immunosuppression, so infection risk."

57.title: Immune Suppression Raises Infection Risk
57.notes:
Screen for TB and hepatitis B and C before starting; update non-live vaccines; monitor blood counts and organ function regularly, and act early on fever or infection signs.

Say: "The theme is immunosuppression, so infection risk."

Know: Screen for TB and hepatitis B/C before biologics. Update vaccines first, especially live vaccines. Monitor CBC and liver and kidney tests. Counsel patients to report fevers early.

58.title: Quick Check
58.notes: Quick check: give 30 seconds, take a show of hands, then reveal.

59.title: Answer
59.notes: Answer: a DMARD modifies the disease process, while an NSAID only masks symptoms.

60.title: Drug Names Reveal the Class: Read the Stem
60.notes:
Teach students to read the stem first: it reveals mechanism class before the drug is recalled.

Say: "Read the stem and you know the class." -mab is a monoclonal antibody. -zumab is humanized, -ximab chimeric, -umab fully human. -cept is a receptor fusion protein. -nib/-tinib is a kinase inhibitor (for example tofacitinib, JAK). -coxib is COX-2 selective. -profen, -fenac and -oxicam are NSAID subclasses.

U2-R1.question: Name the four key inflammatory mediators that sensitize nociceptors and drive musculoskeletal pain.
U2-R1.answer: Prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6).

U2-R2.question: Where in the arachidonic acid pathway do corticosteroids, act compared to NSAIDs? Why does that positioning let corticosteroids suppress a broader range of mediators?

U2-R3.answer: NAPQI; N-acetylcysteine (a glutathione precursor) replenishes glutathione to detoxify NAPQI.

U2-R4.question: Compare COX-1 and COX-2: which one is the "housekeeping" enzyme, and which is the primary source of inflammatory prostaglandins?
U2-R4.answer: COX-1 = housekeeping (gastric protection, renal blood flow); COX-2 = induced at inflammation sites, main source of inflammatory prostaglandins.

U2-R5.question: What trade-off does celecoxib (a COX-2 selective inhibitor) make compared to nonselective NSAIDs?
U2-R5.answer: Lower GI risk, higher cardiovascular risk; renal risk is similar to nonselective NSAIDs.

U2-R6.question: What single feature distinguishes a DMARD from an NSAID in rheumatoid arthritis management?
U2-R6.answer: DMARDs modify the underlying disease process rather than only masking symptoms.

U2-R7.question: Why is methotrexate dosed weekly rather than daily, and what is routinely co-prescribed to reduce its toxicity?
U2-R7.answer: Weekly dosing avoids fatal daily-dose toxicity; folate supplementation reduces hepatotoxicity/marrow suppression/pulmonary toxicity risk.

U2-R8.question: Name one biologic DMARD from each of these categories: TNF inhibitor, IL-6 inhibitor, B-cell targeted therapy, T-cell costimulation modulator. What is the shared major safety risk across all DMARDs (conventional and biologic)?
U2-R8.answer: TNF inhibitor — adalimumab/etanercept/infliximab; IL-6 — tocilizumab; B-cell — rituximab; T-cell costimulation — abatacept; shared risk — immunosuppression/infection.

quiz.stem: In Figure 1, corticosteroids are shown blocking the pathway at the "Membrane Phospholipids → Arachidonic Acid" step, while NSAIDs act one step later. What does this positioning explain?

options.A: Corticosteroids act upstream of NSAIDs, which is why they can suppress a broader range of inflammatory mediators, not just prostaglandins
options.B: Corticosteroids and NSAIDs block the exact same enzyme
options.C: NSAIDs act upstream of corticosteroids
options.D: Neither drug class affects the arachidonic acid pathway

quiz.why: By inhibiting phospholipase A₂, corticosteroids block the release of arachidonic acid itself — upstream of COX — which is why they suppress a broader range of inflammatory mediators (not just prostaglandins) than NSAIDs, which act only at the COX step.

options.D: Cytokines broadly (e.g., all of TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6)

quiz.why: NSAIDs inhibit COX enzymes, directly reducing prostaglandin synthesis. Histamine, bradykinin, and cytokines are important inflammatory mediators too, but they are not the primary target of NSAID mechanism.

quiz.stem: In acetaminophen overdose, hepatotoxicity results primarily from which mechanism?

options.B: Excess Phase II glucuronidation
options.C: Accumulation of NAPQI after glutathione stores are depleted
options.D: Renal crystal formation

quiz.why: NAPQI, normally detoxified by conjugation with glutathione, accumulates once glutathione stores are exhausted in overdose, causing hepatocyte injury — which is why N-acetylcysteine (a glutathione precursor) is the antidote.

tree.name: Part 1 · Musculoskeletal Pain & the Inflammatory Cascade

children.name: Key definitions
facts: **Nociceptive pain:** direct activation of pain receptors by tissue injury.
**Inflammatory pain:** pain driven by inflammatory mediators.
**Neuropathic pain:** pain from nerve injury or dysfunction.
**Acute pain:** recent onset, often tied to an identifiable injury or flare.
**Chronic pain:** persists beyond expected healing time, often > 3 months. Treatment approach differs sharply between acute and chronic pain.

children.name: How it works
facts: **Tissue injury → release of inflammatory mediators → sensitization of nociceptors → pain.**
Key mediators: **prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6).**
Arachidonic acid → COX enzyme → prostaglandins → pain and inflammation: the spine of the acetaminophen, NSAID, and corticosteroid sections.
**NSAIDs and COX-2 inhibitors act at the COX step; glucocorticoids act further upstream; cytokine inhibitors and analgesics act through separate, parallel pathways.**
**Corticosteroids block phospholipase A₂** (membrane phospholipids → arachidonic acid), so a broad range of mediators falls. NSAIDs block only COX, so they lower prostaglandins specifically.
**Nociceptor sensitization:** injury releases PGE2, bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines, which **lower the pain threshold** — normally harmless stimuli now hurt.
Prostaglandins sensitize nociceptors, so they are the main NSAID target; bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines are not blocked by NSAIDs.
Where drugs act: NSAIDs block COX; corticosteroids block PLA2 (phospholipase A₂) one step upstream.
**The immune response:** chronic inflammation involves eicosanoids, leukotrienes, cytokines, chemokines, and many immune cells; RA, SLE, vasculitis, and gout all stem from this cascade.
The lipoxygenase branch of arachidonic acid makes leukotrienes (chemotaxis, bronchoconstriction, vascular permeability) — a separate branch from the COX step NSAIDs block.

children.name: Clinical relevance
facts: Most musculoskeletal pain in this lecture is a mix of nociceptive and inflammatory; pure neuropathic pain belongs to a separate pharmacology unit.
The mediator list is the roadmap for the lecture: NSAIDs target prostaglandins, biologic DMARDs target specific cytokines.

**Therapeutic strategies:** goal 1 is symptom relief and function (NSAIDs and DMARDs); goal 2 is slowing tissue damage, for which DMARDs are absolutely necessary. Response is tracked with indices such as DAS28 in RA.

children.name: Drugs named as examples
facts: Corticosteroids (block phospholipase A₂) vs. NSAIDs and COX-2 inhibitors (block COX): two distinct points of intervention.

children.name: Exam traps
facts: Corticosteroids act **upstream** at phospholipase A₂, not at COX — that is why their effect is broader than an NSAID’s.
The lecture’s drugs target nociceptive and inflammatory pain; neuropathic pain is a different unit.

children.name: Class
facts: Effective analgesia, with a narrow margin in overdose: treats pain and fever well, but is **not an anti-inflammatory drug** the way NSAIDs are.
Acetaminophen leaves inflammation alone; NSAIDs go after it directly.

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: Acetaminophen (the lecture’s single non-NSAID analgesic).

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: **Analgesic effect:** relieves mild-to-moderate pain, with a central mechanism that is still incompletely understood.
**Antipyretic effect:** reduces fever via central effects on the hypothalamic temperature-regulating center.
**Anti-inflammatory effect:** minimal at the periphery — unlike NSAIDs, acetaminophen is not a reliable anti-inflammatory agent.
**Mechanism:** analgesia and antipyresis are mainly central, via reduced CNS prostaglandin synthesis; peripheral anti-inflammatory action is minimal.
Textbook adds: a weak peripheral COX-1/COX-2 inhibitor whose pain relief also involves opioid, cannabinoid, and serotonergic systems.

children.name: Indications
facts: Reasonable first-line for mild osteoarthritis pain.
Generally safer first-line than an NSAID in a patient with NSAID red flags (kidney disease, anticoagulation, older age).
Preferred over aspirin in aspirin allergy, hemophilia, peptic ulcer history, or aspirin-induced bronchospasm; alone it is inadequate for inflammatory conditions such as RA.

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: **Overdose: glutathione stores are depleted, NAPQI accumulates, and hepatocyte injury follows.**
**Overdose cascade:** glucuronidation/sulfation saturate → more drug shunted to CYP2E1 → more NAPQI, glutathione exhausted → NAPQI binds hepatocyte proteins → **centrilobular liver necrosis**.
Ingesting 15 g may be fatal (centrilobular hepatic necrosis); take care with liver disease, heavy alcohol use, or malnutrition.

children.name: Contraindications
facts: **Pearl:** chronic alcohol use and fasting lower GSH and raise risk; both also induce CYP2E1.

children.name: Drug interactions
facts: **Hidden overdose:** many combination cold, flu, and sleep products also contain acetaminophen — **unintentional double-dosing is a leading cause of acetaminophen-related liver injury.**
Combining acetaminophen with an NSAID improves pain control but can potentiate the NSAID’s GI toxicity.

children.name: Pharmacokinetics
facts: Normal handling: acetaminophen → NAPQI (toxic metabolite) → glutathione conjugation → safe excretion.
NAPQI = N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine — the “toxic metabolite” example from Lecture 1’s drug-metabolism section.
**Major route (~90%):** glucuronidation and sulfation → safe urinary excretion.
**Minor route (~5–10%):** CYP2E1 oxidation → NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone-imine), normally neutralized by glutathione (GSH) conjugation at therapeutic doses.
Mostly conjugated to inactive sulfate and glucuronide; half-life 2–3 hours, relatively unaffected by renal function.

children.name: Monitoring
facts: **Always ask about ALL sources of acetaminophen.**
Patients often don’t realize a product contains acetaminophen unless they check the label — reinforce generic-name awareness.
**Acute single ingestion:** plot the acetaminophen level on the **Rumack-Matthew nomogram**; check AST/ALT.
**How to use the nomogram:** draw a level at 4 hours or later after a single acute ingestion and plot it against time since ingestion.
**Above the treatment line:** give NAC. **Below the line:** toxicity unlikely. Example: 8 h, 120 mcg/mL is above the line, so start NAC.
The illustrative treatment line runs from 150 mcg/mL at 4 h, halving every 4 h, to 4.7 mcg/mL at 24 h.
**Limits:** not valid before 4 hours, with an unknown ingestion time, or for staggered, repeated supratherapeutic, or chronic ingestion — use clinical judgment, AST/ALT, and poison control.
Start NAC without waiting if presentation is late or the level is unavailable and the ingestion is significant.
After 24 hours the nomogram is not used: 4.7 mcg/mL is only where the treatment line ends, not a safe cutoff. A detectable level or elevated AST/ALT guides NAC, per protocol or poison control.
Adults: generally no more than 4 g/day — and even 4 g is associated with more liver function test abnormalities.

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: **Antidote: N-acetylcysteine**, a glutathione precursor — it replenishes glutathione to detoxify NAPQI.
Case: a patient on regular acetaminophen for back pain starts an OTC cold-and-flu combination. **What is the hidden danger in this combination?** Double-dosing acetaminophen.
**Antidote: NAC (N-acetylcysteine) replenishes glutathione; give early for best effect.**
Ask: “What is the danger of a cold-and-flu product on top of regular acetaminophen?” Look for unintentional double dosing from combination products.
**Other analgesics — tramadol:** weak μ-opioid agonist plus serotonin/norepinephrine reuptake inhibition; no anti-inflammatory effect; up to 300 mg/day; risks serotonin syndrome and seizures.

children.name: Class
facts: Powerful anti-inflammatory effect, with real systemic risk.
**Nonselective NSAIDs inhibit both COX-1 and COX-2.**
**Celecoxib selectively inhibits COX-2 over COX-1.**

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: Ibuprofen — common first-line choice for mild-moderate pain.
Naproxen — longer half-life, twice-daily dosing.
Diclofenac — available in oral and topical formulations.
Indomethacin — more potent, more GI/CNS adverse effects.
**Ketorolac — short-term use only, significant GI/renal risk.**
Celecoxib — the COX-2 selective agent.

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: NSAID → COX inhibition → ↓ prostaglandins → ↓ pain, inflammation, fever.
**COX-1, the “housekeeping” enzyme:** maintains gastric mucosal protection and normal renal blood flow; inhibiting it causes GI and renal adverse effects.
**COX-2:** induced mainly at sites of inflammation and the primary source of inflammatory prostaglandins; selective inhibition targets inflammation with less GI toxicity.
Simplified teaching model, not an absolute separation: COX-1 and COX-2 functions overlap, and COX-2 is also constitutively expressed in the kidney and elsewhere.
**Pathway:** COX converts arachidonic acid to prostaglandins **and thromboxane A2 (TXA2)**. Less prostaglandin: pain, fever, and inflammation fall. Less TXA2: bleeding risk.
Every NSAID shares the COX mechanism; the side effects follow from losing protective prostaglandins (GI injury, platelet inhibition, renal effects).
**COX-1 is constitutive:** gastric mucosa (protection), platelets (TXA2, clotting), kidney (renal blood flow). **COX-2 is inducible** in inflamed tissue: pain, swelling, fever.
Nonselective NSAIDs block both isoforms, so GI injury is common. Selectivity trades anti-inflammatory benefit against GI and platelet protection.
Celecoxib selectively inhibits inducible COX-2, the main source of inflammatory prostaglandins, and largely spares COX-1 in gastric mucosa — lowering ulcer and bleeding risk.
**Celecoxib’s trade-off:** PGI2 (prostacyclin) falls without a matching drop in TXA2, which raises cardiovascular event risk; stomach and platelet protection continue.
Celecoxib still affects kidney prostaglandins, so renal risk is not eliminated.
Aspirin irreversibly blocks platelet COX (the effect lasts the 8–10-day life of the platelet); other nonselective NSAIDs are reversible inhibitors.
COX-2 inhibitors spare platelet thromboxane (made by COX-1) but block endothelial prostacyclin — so they are not cardioprotective.

children.name: Indications
facts: Oral NSAIDs for osteoarthritis — effective, but carry the systemic risks below.
Topical NSAIDs — effective local relief with much lower systemic exposure.
NSAIDs ease symptoms but, unlike DMARDs, do not alter the course of any arthritic disorder.
Used in RA, spondyloarthropathies, OA, sprains and strains, low back pain, and gout (tolmetin appears ineffective in gout).

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: **Gastrointestinal:** gastritis, peptic ulcer, GI bleeding.
**Renal:** decreased renal perfusion, fluid retention, acute kidney injury.
**Cardiovascular:** hypertension, increased risk of cardiovascular events.
**Celecoxib:** lower risk of ulcer/bleeding, but **COX-2 selectivity is associated with increased cardiovascular event risk — a key trade-off.**
Celecoxib’s renal risk is similar to nonselective NSAIDs — COX-2 selectivity does not protect the kidney.
**GI:** less prostaglandin-driven mucus and bicarbonate leaves the mucosa open to injury (ulcer, bleeding).
**Kidney:** reduced afferent arteriolar dilation lowers renal blood flow (AKI, fluid retention).
**Platelets:** reduced TXA2 impairs aggregation, increasing bleeding risk.
Beyond GI, renal, and CV: headache, tinnitus, dizziness, rare aseptic meningitis, liver test abnormalities, asthma, rashes, hyperkalemia.

children.name: Contraindications
facts: Use caution or avoid in: active GI bleeding or ulcer history; chronic kidney disease; heart failure or cardiovascular disease.
Also caution or avoid with anticoagulant therapy and in late pregnancy.
Ibuprofen is relatively contraindicated with nasal polyps, angioedema, or bronchospastic reactivity to aspirin.

children.name: Drug interactions
facts: NSAIDs + anticoagulants → ↑ bleeding risk.
NSAIDs + ACE inhibitors/ARBs → ↑ AKI risk; add a diuretic and it is the **“triple whammy,”** a very high-yield AKI pattern.
NSAIDs + diuretics → reduced diuretic effect, ↑ renal risk.
NSAIDs + corticosteroids → ↑ GI ulcer risk.
Ibuprofen taken with aspirin blocks aspirin’s irreversible platelet inhibition, limiting its cardioprotective effect.
Celecoxib (a CYP2C9 substrate) occasionally interacts with warfarin and raises lithium and fluconazole levels.

children.name: Pharmacokinetics
facts: Naproxen’s longer half-life allows twice-daily dosing; diclofenac comes as oral and topical forms.
**Chemistry & pharmacokinetics:** most NSAIDs are weak acids, well absorbed, ~98% albumin-bound, metabolized by CYP3A or CYP2C, and renally excreted.

children.name: Monitoring
facts: These three systems (GI, renal, CV) are the organizing framework for every NSAID contraindication and interaction discussion (Table 1).
Highest GI-bleeding risk: celecoxib, or a nonselective NSAID plus omeprazole or misoprostol.

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: Case: a 72-year-old with OA, CKD, hypertension, and an anticoagulant. **Is an NSAID a good first-line choice for this patient’s pain? Why or why not?**
**Three NSAID red flags at once** — renal disease, anticoagulation, and age-related bleeding risk — make acetaminophen or a non-NSAID strategy generally safer first-line.
Celecoxib is a classic “trade one risk for another” point: a better GI profile, but not a free lunch cardiovascularly or renally.
There is no risk-free NSAID choice, only a different risk profile.
**Choice of NSAID:** all are about equally effective, so choose by toxicity, cost, and patient factors; in renal insufficiency nonacetylated salicylates may be best.

children.name: Class
facts: **Osteoarthritis (OA):** primarily degenerative joint disease — cartilage breakdown with mechanical wear.
**Rheumatoid arthritis (RA):** autoimmune, systemic inflammatory disease — immune-mediated joint destruction.
**OA pathophysiology:** mechanical load and wear degrade cartilage; bone remodels with osteophytes.
**RA pathophysiology:** immune activation → autoimmune synovitis forms a **pannus** that erodes cartilage and bone; **TNF-α and IL-6** drive the inflammation and joint damage.
OA treatment goal: pain control and function.
RA treatment goal: suppress disease activity, not just pain.
The hinge: OA is managed mainly with analgesics/NSAIDs, while RA requires disease-modifying therapy.
**DMARD (Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drug):** a drug intended to alter the course of RA, not just mask its symptoms.
**Goal of therapy:** slow or halt joint destruction and systemic inflammation, rather than providing analgesia alone.
An NSAID can make a patient feel better without changing the disease trajectory; a DMARD is meant to change the trajectory itself.
**NSAIDs** relieve pain and swelling within days but do not alter joint damage; **DMARDs** take weeks to months to act, then slow cartilage and bone destruction.
**Timing:** judge a DMARD over months, not after the first visit — set expectations that benefit builds over months. Relief now with NSAIDs, protection later with DMARDs.
Targeted therapy: each biologic class corresponds to a different cytokine or cell type in the inflammatory cascade — the mediator list from the start of the lecture.
DMARD effects take 2 weeks to 6 months to appear. Types: conventional synthetic (cs), biologic (b), and targeted synthetic (ts, e.g., tofacitinib).
Biologics are large molecules, usually proteins made by recombinant DNA technology; JAK inhibitors are oral small-molecule targeted synthetic DMARDs.

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: **Methotrexate — the anchor drug for most RA regimens.**
Hydroxychloroquine — milder disease; relatively favorable safety profile.
Sulfasalazine — often used in combination regimens.
Leflunomide — alternative when methotrexate is not tolerated.
Adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab — **TNF inhibitors**.
Tocilizumab — **IL-6 inhibitor**.
Rituximab — **B-cell targeted therapy**.
Abatacept — **T-cell costimulation modulator**.

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: **Mechanism: inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, reducing immune cell proliferation at low RA doses.** (methotrexate)
**Hydroxychloroquine** alters lysosomal and TLR signaling (less antigen signaling); **sulfasalazine** reduces cytokine and prostaglandin production.
**Leflunomide** inhibits DHODH, blocking pyrimidine synthesis (slower T-cell growth).
Conventional DMARDs act inside cells or on broad immune pathways, with a slower onset than biologics.
**Methotrexate’s folate pathway:** blocking DHFR stops dihydrofolate (DHF) → tetrahydrofolate (THF), the folate needed for purine and thymidylate (DNA) synthesis.
At low RA doses methotrexate is likely anti-inflammatory via **adenosine release**, not cytotoxicity.
TNF inhibitors block tumor necrosis factor-alpha signaling.
IL-6 inhibitors block interleukin-6 receptor signaling.
B-cell targeted therapy depletes or modulates B lymphocytes.
T-cell costimulation modulators block the second signal needed for T-cell activation.
Figure 3: abatacept acts at T-cell activation, TNF inhibitors and tocilizumab at cytokine release, rituximab at B cells — all upstream of synovial inflammation and joint destruction.
**TNF inhibitors:** antibodies (infliximab, adalimumab) and etanercept, a receptor fusion protein, neutralize soluble and membrane TNF-α, preventing TNFR activation.
**Tocilizumab** blocks both membrane and soluble IL-6 receptors.
**Abatacept (CTLA-4-Ig)** binds CD80/86 and blocks CD28 costimulation, acting early at T-cell activation.
**Rituximab (anti-CD20)** binds CD20 and depletes B cells for months.
Each biologic intercepts a different step of the immune cascade: walk it from T-cell activation to cytokines to synovial damage — abatacept acts earliest.

children.name: Indications
facts: **OA step 1:** acetaminophen — reasonable first-line for mild OA pain.
**OA step 2:** oral NSAIDs (effective, systemic risks) or topical NSAIDs (local relief, much lower systemic exposure).
**Intra-articular corticosteroid injections:** short-term relief for flares in a single joint.
Other approaches: activity modification, physical therapy, weight management.
**Where each OA analgesic acts:** acetaminophen centrally (brain and spinal cord COX) — little anti-inflammatory effect in the joint.
Oral or topical NSAIDs block COX in joint tissue (synovium and cartilage), lowering prostaglandins, pain, and swelling.
An intra-articular steroid calms local inflammation inside the joint for fast, short-term flare relief. Choice depends on which tissue drives the pain.
Methotrexate anchors most RA regimens; leflunomide is the alternative when it is not tolerated.
Rheumatoid arthritis: they modify the disease course rather than only masking symptoms.
TNF inhibitors are the first-line biologic; tocilizumab works as monotherapy; rituximab is used after TNF-inhibitor failure.
**Glucocorticoid drugs in rheumatic diseases:** used chronically in 30–70% of RA patients; relief is prompt and dramatic, and they slow new bone erosions.
Long-term prednisone in RA: no more than 7.5 mg daily, tapered when possible — even 2.8 mg daily for over 5 years is linked to severe infections.
Intra-articular corticosteroids often relieve painful symptoms for up to several months.
Long-term glucocorticoid harms: osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, Cushing syndrome, infections, cataract, glaucoma, gastric ulcer, depression.
Methotrexate starts at 7.5 mg weekly and rises to 15–25 mg weekly; it slows new erosions in RA.
**Combination therapy with DMARDs** is now the rule when monotherapy falls short; triple therapy (methotrexate, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine) rivals etanercept plus methotrexate.

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: **Boxed warning — all TNF inhibitors:** possible malignancy, especially lymphoma.
**Boxed warning — all JAK inhibitors:** venous thromboembolism (DVT, PE), major adverse cardiovascular events, and cancer.
Methotrexate key adverse effects: **hepatotoxicity, bone marrow suppression, pulmonary toxicity.**
**The major safety theme across all DMARDs: immunosuppression → increased infection risk.** This holds for conventional and biologic DMARDs alike.
**Risk:** suppressed immunity lets latent TB and opportunistic infections (TB, viral, fungal) emerge.
TNF inhibitors: watch for reactivation of latent TB. Tocilizumab can raise lipids and liver enzymes. Abatacept has a generally lower infection signal.
Methotrexate’s most common toxicities are nausea and stomatitis; dose-related liver enzyme elevations are frequent.
TNF inhibitors: TB reactivation, fungal infections, hepatitis B reactivation, new or worse heart failure, demyelinating disease, lupus-like syndrome.

children.name: Contraindications
facts: **Methotrexate is contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic).**
Don’t stack biologics: abatacept with a TNF inhibitor probably raises serious infections; upadacitinib with biologic DMARDs is not recommended.

children.name: Drug interactions
facts: Hydroxychloroquine can reduce methotrexate clearance.
Tocilizumab stimulates CYP450 — doses of cyclosporine or warfarin may need adjusting.
Methotrexate given with TNF inhibitors reduces anti-drug antibodies (infliximab, golimumab, certolizumab).

children.name: Pharmacokinetics
facts: **Methotrexate is dosed weekly (not daily) — a critical patient-safety point, since daily dosing can be fatal.**
**Weekly dosing only:** daily dosing has caused fatal toxicity.

children.name: Monitoring
facts: **Folate supplementation** is routinely co-prescribed with methotrexate to reduce toxicity.
Folic acid co-therapy reduces methotrexate’s liver, marrow, lung, and GI toxicity.
**Baseline screening:** e.g., tuberculosis and hepatitis B/C screening before starting biologics.
**Vaccination:** update vaccines, especially live vaccines, before starting therapy.
**Ongoing monitoring:** regular labs to catch cytopenias, hepatotoxicity, or infection early.
**Infection precautions:** counsel patients to report fevers or infection symptoms promptly.
**Screen first:** TB test (IGRA or TST) and hepatitis B and C serology before starting; check hepatitis B before rituximab.
**Vaccines:** update non-live vaccines before treatment.
**Monitor:** CBC and liver and kidney labs every 1–3 months; act early on fever or infection signs.
Folic acid or leucovorin reduces stomatitis, GI, and liver test problems but may cut methotrexate efficacy by 10–18%.
Hydroxychloroquine: baseline eye exam, then annual screening after 5 years (retinopathy).
Avoid live vaccines for up to 3 months after stopping abatacept; stop upadacitinib before a live attenuated vaccine.

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: A 72-year-old with OA, CKD, hypertension, and an anticoagulant: acetaminophen or a non-NSAID strategy first.
OA and RA both affect the joint but are two very different diseases — don’t give RA patients analgesia alone.
Methotrexate’s weekly dosing is one of the highest-yield patient-safety points in all of rheumatology pharmacology.
Match each generic name to its class: adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab (TNF); tocilizumab (IL-6); rituximab (B cell); abatacept (T-cell costimulation).

**Read the stem first:** it reveals the mechanism class before the drug is recalled (-mab antibody: -zumab humanized, -ximab chimeric, -umab fully human; -cept receptor fusion; -nib/-tinib kinase inhibitor; -coxib COX-2 selective; -profen, -fenac, -oxicam NSAID subclasses).
Topical diclofenac 1% gel is sold over the counter for OA and muscular pain.
**Biosimilars:** near-copies of legacy biologics with the same efficacy, toxicity, and immunogenicity at potentially lower cost.
If methotrexate alone falls short: add csDMARDs or a biologic — usually a TNF inhibitor first, then non-TNF biologics or JAK inhibitors.

brief.part: Part 1 · Musculoskeletal Pain & the Inflammatory Cascade
hy: Injury → mediators → nociceptor sensitization → pain.
Musculoskeletal pain is driven by inflammatory mediators (prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, cytokines) — NSAIDs and corticosteroids intervene at different points along this cascade.
Corticosteroids = phospholipase A₂ (broad); NSAIDs = COX (prostaglandins).
Prostaglandins drive inflammatory pain, and COX makes them.
traps: Corticosteroids act **upstream** at phospholipase A₂, not at COX — that is why their effect is broader than an NSAID’s.
The lecture’s drugs target nociceptive and inflammatory pain; neuropathic pain is a different unit.

hy: Acetaminophen treats pain and fever but is not a reliable anti-inflammatory agent; its overdose toxicity is mediated by NAPQI accumulation.
Overdose: glutathione depleted → NAPQI → hepatocyte injury.
Antidote: N-acetylcysteine (glutathione precursor).
Ask about ALL sources — combination cold/flu/sleep products hide acetaminophen.
Acetaminophen is central, with no real anti-inflammatory effect. Overdose means NAPQI, and the antidote is NAC.
COX-1 = housekeeping (gastric protection, renal blood flow); COX-2 = inflammation.
NSAIDs are effective but carry real GI, renal, and cardiovascular risk; celecoxib trades GI risk for cardiovascular risk (renal risk similar).
NSAID harms: GI, renal, cardiovascular.
Triple whammy: NSAID + ACEi/ARB + diuretic → AKI.
Ketorolac: short-term only; significant GI/renal risk.
COX-1 protects the stomach, platelets and kidney. Nonselective NSAIDs block both isoforms.
Celecoxib cuts GI risk but raises cardiovascular risk, and does not spare the kidney.
OA = degenerative → pain control; RA = autoimmune → suppress disease activity.
OA ladder: acetaminophen → oral or topical NSAIDs → intra-articular steroids for a single-joint flare.
DMARDs (conventional and biologic — methotrexate, adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, tocilizumab, rituximab, abatacept) modify RA’s disease course rather than only masking symptoms.
Methotrexate: DHFR inhibitor, **weekly**, with folate.
Methotrexate toxicity: liver, marrow, lung; teratogenic.
HCQ = milder RA; sulfasalazine = combinations; leflunomide = if MTX not tolerated.
DMARDs change disease. Methotrexate is weekly, and screen for TB and hepatitis before biologics.
TNF: adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab · IL-6: tocilizumab · B cell: rituximab · T-cell costimulation: abatacept.
Shared risk: immunosuppression → infection.
Before biologics: TB + hepatitis B/C screening, update (live) vaccines.
